title: Citizens to Preserve Overton Park, Inc. v. Volpe
lead: A federally funded highway route through a Memphis park receives approval without stated findings, and residents ask the courts to examine whether the Secretary actually applied Congress’s park-protection requirements.

actors.name: Citizens and conservation organizations
actors.role: Challenged approval of the Interstate 40 segment through Overton Park.

actors.name: John Volpe, Secretary of Transportation
actors.role: Federal official responsible for the statutory approval decision.

actors.name: Tennessee and Memphis officials
actors.role: Participated in route planning and land acquisition.

proceedings: The action began in the District of Columbia and was transferred to the Western District of Tennessee.
The district court granted the Secretary summary judgment; the Sixth Circuit affirmed.
The Supreme Court stayed construction, reversed, and remanded for district-court review of the administrative record.
limits: The Court did not resolve conflicting route and design evidence or finally prohibit the highway. The later litigation discussed by the assigned editors is distinguished from this 1971 judgment, and the account does not certify present highway law.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: A long-planned expressway encounters new protections for parkland
sections.cue: What would the route do, and what did Congress require before approval?
paragraphs: Overton Park occupied 342 acres near central Memphis, with recreational facilities, a zoo, and approximately 170 acres of forest. Planners proposed a six-lane Interstate 40 segment that would take twenty-six acres and separate the zoo from the rest of the park. Most of the road would be depressed, except where it crossed a creek. Federal officials approved earlier planning stages before the relevant park-protection legislation.

Congress then enacted § 4(f) of the Department of Transportation Act and § 138 of the Federal-Aid Highway Act. The provisions barred approval of a federally funded project using public parkland unless no feasible and prudent alternative existed and the project incorporated all possible planning to minimize harm. State and local preferences did not eliminate the federal Secretary of Transportation’s independent responsibility under those provisions.

After the requirements became applicable, the Secretary announced concurrence in the local route choice in April 1968. Tennessee acquired the right-of-way in 1969, and final route and design approval followed in November. Neither announcement contained findings explaining why alternatives or additional harm-reduction measures were insufficient.

sections.title: Residents challenge the approval and lose on litigation affidavits
sections.cue: What was contested rather than established?
paragraphs: Private citizens and local and national conservation organizations challenged the approval, naming Secretary John Volpe as respondent. They asserted that routes north or south of the park were feasible and prudent and proposed tunneling or drainage methods to reduce harm if the park route remained. They also questioned whether the Secretary had independently evaluated the project or merely accepted local views.

The action began in the District of Columbia and, at the Secretary’s request, moved to the Western District of Tennessee. The government submitted affidavits prepared for litigation to defend the approval. The petitioners offered contrary affidavits and sought to depose a former Federal Highway Administrator. These competing assertions did not establish that any proposed alternative was suitable.

The district court granted summary judgment for the Secretary. It found no requirement for formal findings, rejected the deposition as an intrusion into administrative mental processes, and considered the affidavits insufficient to show action outside the Secretary’s broad authority. The Sixth Circuit affirmed. The Supreme Court stayed construction and expedited review.

sections.title: The Court finds a legal standard in Congress’s protective command
sections.cue: Why was this decision reviewable despite administrative discretion?
paragraphs: Justice Marshall wrote the Court’s opinion, which Justice Stewart announced. The Court first separated reviewability under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) § 701 from the standards of review under § 706. Congress had not prohibited review. Section 701(a)(2)’s exception for action committed to agency discretion was narrow, and these statutes contained a prohibition with defined exceptions: no feasible and prudent alternative and all possible harm-minimizing planning. Those requirements supplied law for a court to apply.

The government conceded that feasibility concerned sound engineering. It sought broader balancing under prudence, including cost and community disruption. The Court answered that ordinary cost savings and avoidance of displacement would routinely favor publicly owned parkland. If those considerations had equal weight with preservation, the statute would do little. Congress made park preservation paramount unless alternatives presented unusual problems or costs or disruption of extraordinary magnitude.

The Secretary therefore had to exercise independent federal judgment, looking beyond what state and local officials supplied. Whether the Secretary had actually done so remained to be examined; the Supreme Court did not resolve the competing affidavits.

sections.title: The Court specifies searching review without a new route-selection trial
sections.cue: Which inquiries did the district court still owe?
paragraphs: This approval concerned funding and a particular route, not a decision on an adjudicatory hearing record required by statute. The local public hearing informed residents and collected their views; it did not create the exclusive evidentiary basis for the federal decision. Substantial-evidence review under § 706(2)(E) did not govern, and the circumstances permitting trial de novo under § 706(2)(F) were absent. The opinion’s compressed discussion of rulemaking cannot be read to put every notice-and-comment rule under substantial-evidence review; the statutory provision concerned proceedings under §§ 556–557 or otherwise reviewed on the record of a statutorily provided hearing.

The district court first had to identify the narrow choices Congress permitted and determine whether the Secretary reasonably could place the facts within those bounds. It next had to examine whether the decision considered relevant factors and reflected a clear error of judgment under arbitrary-or-capricious review. Finally, it had to test compliance with applicable procedures. A presumption of regularity excused none of those inquiries.

The examination had to be careful and searching while leaving the choice within lawful bounds to the Secretary. “Plenary” review on remand did not authorize the district judge to conduct a new trial to select a preferred route.

sections.title: Missing formal findings do not excuse reliance on reconstructed reasons
sections.cue: What record and explanation could the court demand?
paragraphs: Neither park statute required formal findings, and the APA’s formal-findings provisions did not apply. The decision was clear as to what route and design the Secretary approved. Its support and explanation remained the problem; absence of a document labeled findings was not itself dispositive.

A later departmental order, DOT Order 5610.1, required formal findings. The petitioners invoked the principle of applying the law effective at appellate decision. The Court considered intervening land acquisition and clearing and the prospect of prompt review on the existing administrative record. It declined to order an automatic remand to the Secretary solely for formal findings under that later order.

The litigation affidavits nevertheless could not substitute for the full record before the Secretary when he acted. They defended the decision in court and risked reconstructing its rationale. The district court had to start with the contemporaneous administrative record.

If that record did not disclose the factors considered or their treatment, the district court could obtain necessary explanation, including testimony from participating officials. Inquiry into mental processes ordinarily should be avoided; when contemporaneous findings exist, a strong showing of bad faith or improper behavior is needed. Here, lacking formal findings, explanatory testimony might be indispensable. Alternatively, the Secretary could prepare findings. The court had to assess any retrospective explanation critically, illuminating the decision actually made without allowing entirely new justifications. The majority left the choice of an effective and expeditious method to the district court, not an unrestricted right to depose every official.

sections.title: The Court orders record review while two Justices prefer a new agency proceeding
sections.cue: How did the separate opinions differ about the remand?
paragraphs: On March 2, 1971, the Supreme Court reversed and remanded for district-court review on the full administrative record. It did not hold that a particular alternative route was feasible and prudent, order a tunnel, or finally prohibit the highway.

Justice Black, joined by Justice Brennan, agreed with reversal but would return the entire matter directly to the Secretary. Black believed the Secretary had not performed the statutory duty at all and should undertake the necessary hearing, findings, and policy determinations. Whether findings were called formal or informal did not matter to him. His conclusion of an existing failure was stronger than the majority’s direction to examine adequately what had occurred.

Justice Blackmun fully joined the majority and added a statement. More than a decade of planning by successive officials preceded the new statutory requirements of 1966 and 1968. That history explained the sparse record, in his view, without excusing the ordered review. Justice Douglas did not participate. Six Justices joined the majority, with Black and Brennan agreeing on reversal but favoring a different remedy.

sections.title: The casebook follows the remand into later administrative-law questions
sections.cue: Which later observations belong to the editors?
paragraphs: The four assigned notes, pages 889–895, examine informal action, administrative records, reasons, and bad faith. The first highlights review despite the absence of a specially prescribed agency procedure or an express review statute for that particular decision. The second considers how judicial review encourages record-making and administrative routines. It also describes subsequent litigation: the Secretary later refused to approve the park route, and the Sixth Circuit rejected a requirement that the Secretary name an alternative before refusing. Those are later events reported by the editors, not the Supreme Court’s immediate disposition.

The third note connects Chenery I’s insistence on the agency’s actual reasons with Overton Park’s allowance of critically assessed later explanation. Counsel cannot invent an agency policy rationale. The fourth discusses the 2019 census litigation in Department of Commerce v. New York, including the enlarged record, discovery, and differing coalitions concerning reasonableness and the contrived explanation. The editors caution that every motive need not be disclosed and question that later decision’s reach. Their comparisons and critiques retain the other cases’ independent source-review statuses and are not additional holdings of Overton Park.
